target:
def Target : Prop :=
  ∃ (Q : S1 Bool Bool → Prop) (c4 : (List Bool → Bool) → Prop),
    (∀ N, N.D9 → ¬ Q N) ∧ (∃ N, Q N) ∧
    ∀ N : S1 Bool Bool, (Q N ↔ c4 N.d4)
a_raw: {"translation": "Target defines a proposition (it does not assert or prove it). First, a system N of type S1 Bool Bool consists of: a finite type of nodes (which may be empty); for each node n, an arbitrary state type (not required to be finite); an initial global state assigning a state to each node; for each node n, an update function taking a global state and a Boolean input and returning a next state for n; and an output function taking a global state and returning a Boolean. Its input-output function N.d4 : List Bool → Bool sends any finite sequence of Booleans to the Boolean obtained by starting from the initial global state, synchronously updating all nodes' states step by step from left to right for each input in the sequence, and applying the output function to the final global state (or to the initial global state for the empty sequence). Its dependency relation has a directed edge from node m to node n iff there exist two arbitrary global states (not required to be reachable from the initial state) that agree on every node other than m, and a Boolean input, on which n's update function produces different next states. The acyclicity condition N.D9 states that no node has a nonempty directed path to itself (length ≥ 1, including self-loops) in this dependency relation. The proposition Target states that there exist an arbitrary predicate Q on systems of type S1 Bool Bool and an arbitrary predicate c4 on functions List Bool → Bool (with no extra requirements such as decidability or computability) such that: (1) for every system N of type S1 Bool Bool, if N satisfies the acyclicity condition N.D9, then Q N is false; (2) there exists at least one system N of type S1 Bool Bool such that Q N holds; and (3) for every system N of type S1 Bool Bool, Q N holds if and only if c4 holds of N's input-output function N.d4."}
translation: Target defines a proposition (it does not assert or prove it). First, a system N of type S1 Bool Bool consists of: a finite type of nodes (which may be empty); for each node n, an arbitrary state type (not required to be finite); an initial global state assigning a state to each node; for each node n, an update function taking a global state and a Boolean input and returning a next state for n; and an output function taking a global state and returning a Boolean. Its input-output function N.d4 : List Bool → Bool sends any finite sequence of Booleans to the Boolean obtained by starting from the initial global state, synchronously updating all nodes' states step by step from left to right for each input in the sequence, and applying the output function to the final global state (or to the initial global state for the empty sequence). Its dependency relation has a directed edge from node m to node n iff there exist two arbitrary global states (not required to be reachable from the initial state) that agree on every node other than m, and a Boolean input, on which n's update function produces different next states. The acyclicity condition N.D9 states that no node has a nonempty directed path to itself (length ≥ 1, including self-loops) in this dependency relation. The proposition Target states that there exist an arbitrary predicate Q on systems of type S1 Bool Bool and an arbitrary predicate c4 on functions List Bool → Bool (with no extra requirements such as decidability or computability) such that: (1) for every system N of type S1 Bool Bool, if N satisfies the acyclicity condition N.D9, then Q N is false; (2) there exists at least one system N of type S1 Bool Bool such that Q N holds; and (3) for every system N of type S1 Bool Bool, Q N holds if and only if c4 holds of N's input-output function N.d4.

divergences.description: The description speaks simply of 'systems with Boolean inputs and outputs', whereas S1 Bool Bool restricts to discrete-time, deterministic, synchronous, time-invariant (fixed-parameter) machines with a fixed initial state, arbitrary (possibly infinite) per-node state types, and a finite set of nodes (Fintype A1). The finite-node restriction is mathematically load-bearing (an infinite-node acyclic network could realize any List Bool -> Bool function, falsifying Target), though it is a standard idealization for neural-network systems in the unfolding-argument literature.

The loop-free condition D9 defines node-to-node dependencies (D7/D8) by quantifying over all global states, including states unreachable from the initial state a4. Consequently, a system whose dependency cycles occur only on unreachable states does not satisfy D9 and is not excluded from Q by the feedforward clause.

The description cites 'P2 at each finite horizon' as 'the scope O'Reilly-Shah et al. describe', omitting the second constraint explicitly named in [P-O1] ('functional input-output equivalence over finite time horizons with fixed parameters', where O'Reilly-Shah et al.'s own critique targets the fixed-parameters constraint via plasticity). Because S1 already enforces fixed parameters, this is only a minor omission in summarizing [P-O1].

judgement.summary: Target accurately formalizes the author's description—an existential statement of a Boolean-I/O system verdict and an unbounded input-output predicate agreeing on all systems while excluding all acyclic ones—and the stated logical relation to P2 (unbounded vs. finite-horizon) and the passages is accurate. The only caveats are minor unstated modeling idealizations in S1 and D9 (notably the load-bearing finite-node assumption) and omitting 'with fixed parameters' when citing the scope described in [P-O1].
